chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, and Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, both together, from Ibn Mahboub, from Khadir al-Sayrafi, from Bureyd ibn Muawiya al-Ajaly, who said:

Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) was asked about a man who killed a man deliberately, so the legal penalty was not established upon him, and the testimony was not valid against him, until he became mad and his intellect went away. Then another group testified against him after he had gone mad that he had killed him. He (peace be upon him) said: If they testify against him that he killed him when he killed him, and he was sound, with no reason from the spoiling of his intellect, he would be killed due to it. And if they testify against him with that, and there was known wealth for him, the wergild would be handed over to the inheritors of the killed one from the wealth of the killer. And if he did not leave wealth, the wergild would be given from the public treasury, and the blood of a Muslim man would not be invalidated.

key_terms.قُتِلَ بِهِ: Killed due to it (execution for murder)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a deliberate killer who goes mad before the penalty is established?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi clarifies the jurisprudential distinction between the time of the act and the time of judgment, emphasizing that sanity at the moment of killing establishes liability even if insanity follows. It details the practical application of qisas (retaliation) versus diyah (blood money), ensuring that a Muslim's blood is not nullified by procedural delays or subsequent mental incapacity. This ruling reflects the Shia emphasis on the continuity of legal responsibility despite changes in the defendant's state.

en.hubeali: Muhammad Bin Yahya, from Ahmad Bin Muhammad, and Ali Bin Ibrahim, from his father, both together from Ibn Mahboub, from Hazir Al Sayrafi, from Bureyd Bin Muawiya Al Ajaly who said,

‘Abu Ja’farasws was asked about a man who killed a man deliberately. So the legal penalty (Hadd) had not been established upon him, and the testimonies had not been reckoned against him, he became mad and his intellect went away. Then another group testified against him after he had gone mad that he had killed him’. (Heasws) said: ‘When he killed him, he was correct, there was no reason from the spoiling of his intellect, (thus) he would be killed due to it. And if he is testified against with that, and there was known wealth for him, it would be handed over to the inheritors of the killed one. The wergild is from the wealth of the killer. And if he did not leave wealth, the wergild would be given from the public treasury, and there would be no invalidation of the blood of a Muslim person’.
